Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 65, verse 1:

﴿O Prophet, when you divorce women﴾ If it is asked: why was the Prophet ﷺ addressed alone, and then the address came in the plural? The answer: since the ruling on divorce is shared by the Prophet ﷺ and his community, it was said: "If you (plural) divorce," as an address to him and to them together. He ﷺ was singled out with the vocative as a mark of honour, as one says to the leader and chief of a people: "O so-and-so, do (plural)," meaning: do you and your people. Also, the Prophet ﷺ is the one who conveys (the message) to his community, so it is as if He said: "O Prophet, when you and your community divorce." It was also said: its sense is "O Prophet, tell your community: when you divorce." This is weak, because it implies that this ruling is specific to his community and not to him. It was also said: the Prophet ﷺ was addressed with "divorce you (plural)" as a mark of honour to him, as you say to an honoured man: "You (plural) did it." This too is weak, because it implies that the ruling is specific to him ﷺ and not to his community. The meaning of "when you divorce" here is: when you intend to divorce.

There is a difference of opinion as to whether divorce is permissible (mubah) or disliked (makruh). As for divorce not in accordance with the Sunnah (sunnah, the prophetic way), it is forbidden, but it takes effect. As for swearing by divorce, it is forbidden. ﴿So divorce them for their waiting period﴾. Its meaning: divorce them at the start of their waiting period (mustaqbilat li-'iddatihinna). For this reason ʿUthman, Ibn ʿAbbas and Ubayy ibn Kaʿb read: "divorce them at the beginning (fi qubul) of their waiting period," and Ibn ʿUmar read: "li-qubul ʿiddatihinna," and both readings are related from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The meaning of all of this: he should not divorce her while she is menstruating. This is prohibited by consensus, because if he does so the divorce does not fall in the state that God commanded, which is the beginning of the waiting period. There is a difference of opinion as to whether the prohibition of divorce during menstruation is due to lengthening the waiting period, or is an act of worship (ta'abbud). The correct view is that it has a reason, namely that. Branching from this difference are issues: is it permissible if the woman consents or not? Is it permissible to divorce her while she is pregnant or not? Is it permissible to divorce her before consummation while she is menstruating or not? The reasoning of lengthening the waiting period implies permissibility of these branches, while the view of worship implies prohibition. Whoever divorces during menstruation, the divorce takes effect, and then he is commanded to take her back by compulsion according to Malik, and without compulsion according to al-Shafiʿi, until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure, and then, if he wishes, he divorces, and if he wishes, he keeps her, as reported in the hadith of Ibn ʿUmar, "when he divorced his wife while she was menstruating, and ʿUmar mentioned that to the Prophet ﷺ, and he said to him: 'Order him to take her back until she becomes pure, then menstruates, then becomes pure; then if he wishes he may divorce, and if he wishes he may keep her.'" Malik stipulated that he divorce her in a purity in which he did not touch her, so that the purity is counted, for if he divorces her in a purity after having had intercourse with her in it, one does not know whether she observes the waiting period by delivery or by menstrual cycles, so it is not a divorce for her waiting period as God commanded. ﴿And count the waiting period﴾: he was commanded to do so because of the rulings that depend on it, concerning the right of return, residence, inheritance and other things.

﴿Do not expel them from their houses, nor should they leave﴾. God, glory be to Him, forbade a man to expel the divorced woman from the dwelling in which he divorced her, and forbade her to leave of her own choice, so it is not permissible for her to spend the night outside her house, nor to be absent from it by day except for a necessity of business; this is to preserve lineage and protect the woman. If the dwelling is owned by the husband, or rented by him, he is obliged to house her in it; if the dwelling is hers, he is obliged to pay its rent for the period of the waiting period, and if she had enjoyed it during the marriage, then there are two opinions in the school as to whether she must leave at the end of the waiting period; the sound view is that she must, because the obstacle has ended with the divorce. ﴿Unless they commit a clear immorality﴾. Scholars differ as to what this immorality is that permits the woman in waiting period to leave, on five views. First: it is fornication, so she leaves to be subjected to the prescribed penalty (hadd), related by al-Layth ibn Saʿd and al-Shaʿbi. Second: it is bad speech toward in-laws, so she leaves and her right to residence falls away, and she is obliged to reside in a dwelling she takes for the preservation of lineage; related by Ibn ʿAbbas, and supported by the reading of Ubayy ibn Kaʿb: "unless they behave indecently toward you." Third: it is all sins, such as slander, fornication, theft and other things, so whenever she does any of these her right to residence falls away; also related from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Tabari inclined to it. Fourth: it is leaving her house by way of relocation, so whenever she does that her right to residence falls away; related by Ibn al-Faras, and Malik held this regarding a woman who rebels (nushuz) during the waiting period. Fifth: it is rebellion before the divorce, so if he divorces her because of her rebellion, there is no residence owed to her; related by Qatadah.

﴿You do not know, perhaps God will bring about after that some matter﴾. What is meant by it is return (ruj'ah) according to the majority: that is, count the waiting period and comply with what you were commanded, perhaps God will bring about return to your wives. It was also said: the cause of the return mentioned in the verse was the Prophet ﷺ divorcing Hafsah bint ʿUmar, and God commanded him to take her back.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 65, verses 2–3:

﴿Then when they reach their term, retain them in kindness or part from them in kindness.﴾ He means the end of the waiting period (*'iddah*). Retaining in kindness means good treatment and full provision of maintenance. Parting in kindness means paying the dowry, giving a gift (*mut'ah*) at the time of divorce, fulfilling the conditions, and similar things. ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you.﴾ This is addressed to the husbands. The command refers to calling witnesses to the return (*raj'ah*, the revocation of a divorce during the waiting period) according to the majority of scholars. There are two opinions within the school (*madhhab*) on whether it is obligatory or recommended. Ibn 'Abbas said it refers to witnessing both the divorce and the return. This is the more apparent view, because calling witnesses removes doubt and dispute. There is no difference in this between the return and the divorce. We have discussed the meaning of justice (*'adalah*) in al-Baqarah. The words ﴿just men﴾ indicate that men, not women, testify in divorce and marriage. This is the position of Malik, unlike those who permit women's testimony in these matters. The words ﴿from among you﴾ mean from among the Muslims. It is also said they mean from among the free, and from this is derived the rejection of the testimony of slaves, which is the position of Malik. ﴿And establish the testimony for Allah.﴾ This is addressed to the witnesses. Establishing testimony may mean standing by it: when one is called upon to witness, it becomes obligatory for him to bear witness, and this is a collective obligation (*fard kifayah*, an obligation which is discharged when enough people perform it). Ibn al-Faras pointed to this meaning. It may also mean establishing it with the truth, without bias or self-interest, and al-Zamakhshari explained it this way. This is the more apparent meaning because of the phrase ﴿for Allah﴾, and it is like His saying: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for Allah﴾ (An-Nisa 135). ﴿That﴾ refers to the rulings mentioned above.

﴿And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out.﴾ It is said this refers to divorce, and its meaning is: whoever fears Allah by divorcing with a single pronouncement, as the Sunnah requires, Allah will make for him a way out by permitting the return (*raj'ah*) whenever he regrets the divorce. In this sense it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said to a man who had divorced his wife three times: "You did not fear Allah, so your wife has become separated from you, and I do not see a way out for you," meaning there is no return for you. It is also said that the verse is general, meaning: whoever fears Allah in his words and actions, Allah will make for him a way out from the distress of this world and the Hereafter. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, and this view is preferred for five reasons. First, the wording is taken in its general sense, so divorce and other matters are included. Second, it is reported that it was revealed concerning 'Awf ibn Malik al-Ashja'i, whose son was captured and whose provision was constricted. He complained of this to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who commanded him to be mindful of Allah. He did not wait long before his son was released and Allah widened his provision. Third, it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited it and said: "a way out from the doubts of this world, from the agonies of death, and from the hardships of the Day of Resurrection." Fourth, it is reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I know a verse which, if people adopted it, would suffice them: 'And whoever fears Allah, He will make for him a way out'," and he kept reciting it and repeating it. Fifth, His saying: ﴿and provide for him from where he does not expect﴾, for this does not fit divorce but fits piety in general.

Some scholars said: provision is of two kinds. The first is guaranteed provision for every living being throughout its life, which is the sustenance by which life is sustained, and to it refers His saying: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon Allah﴾ (Hud 6). The second is provision promised specifically to the God-fearing, which is what is mentioned in this verse: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah, then He is sufficient for him﴾, meaning He suffices him, so that he needs nothing else with Him. We have discussed reliance upon Allah (*tawakkul*) in Al 'Imran.

﴿Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose.﴾ He reaches whatever He wills, and nothing can overpower Him. This is an incitement to reliance upon Allah and its confirmation, because when the servant realizes that all affairs are in the hand of Allah, he relies upon Him alone and does not depend upon anyone else. ﴿Allah has already set for everything a measure.﴾ That is, a known extent and a specified time.

It was reported that when the words of Allah, ﴿And divorced women shall wait by themselves for three periods (quru')﴾ [al-Baqarah: 228], were revealed, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the 'iddah (waiting period) of one who has no quru' because of youth or old age?" Then this verse was revealed, making clear that a divorced woman who does not menstruate has an 'iddah of three months. So His words, ﴿and those of your women who have despaired of menstruation﴾, mean: those whose menstruation has stopped because of their advanced age. His words, ﴿and those who have not menstruated﴾, mean: the young girl who has not reached the age of menstruation. This is either conjoined to "those who have despaired" or is a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted, the sense being "and those who have not menstruated likewise." His words, ﴿if you are in doubt﴾, come from ar-rayb (doubt), meaning shakk (uncertainty). Regarding its meaning there are two opinions. The first: if you are in doubt about the ruling on her 'iddah, know that it is three months. The second: if you are in doubt about her menstruation, whether it has stopped or not. According to the first interpretation, it refers to the one whose menstruation has stopped because of her old age, as we have mentioned, and this is the correct view. According to the second interpretation, it refers to the woman in doubt (al-murtabah), the one whose menstruation has become absent while she is of an age in which women menstruate. The scholars have differed regarding her 'iddah, in three opinions. The first: it is three months only, as the verse implies under this interpretation. The second: it is three months after nine months, during which she seeks to ascertain (istibra') that there is no pregnancy, and this is the position of Malik, whose model in this was 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). The third: she observes her 'iddah by the periods (quru') even if she remains thirty years, until she reaches the age of one who does not menstruate, and this is the position of al-Shafi'i and Abu Hanifah.

﴿And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth to their burden﴾. This verse, according to Malik, al-Shafi'i, Abu Hanifah and all the other scholars, is general, concerning both divorced women and widows. So whenever one of them is pregnant, her 'iddah is the delivery of her child. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib and Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse concerns only divorced pregnant women, so they are the ones whose 'iddah is the delivery of their child. As for a widow who is pregnant, according to these two, her 'iddah is the later of the two terms: either delivery or the completion of four months and ten days. The evidence of the majority is the hadith of Subay'ah al-Aslamiyyah, that she was the wife of Sa'd ibn Khawlah, who died while she was pregnant during the Farewell Pilgrimage. When she gave birth, Abu as-Sanabil ibn Ba'kak proposed to her, so she asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he said to her: "Marry whomever you wish." It is mentioned that Ibn 'Abbas returned to this hadith when it reached him, and if it had reached 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him), he would have returned to it too. 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud said: this verse, revealed in the shorter Surat al-Nisa' (meaning Surat al-Talaq), was revealed after the verse in al-Baqarah: ﴿And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves four months and ten days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 234]. Hence it specifies that verse, as the majority of scholars have said.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 65, verse 6:

﴿Lodge them where you dwell, according to your means.﴾ God commanded that divorced women be lodged for the duration of the waiting period (ʿidda). As for a woman divorced by a revocable divorce, lodging and maintenance are obligatory for her upon her husband by consensus. As for a woman divorced irrevocably (mabtūta), there are three opinions. The first: lodging is obligatory for her, but not maintenance; this is the position of Mālik and al-Shāfiʿī. The second: lodging and maintenance are both obligatory for her; this is the position of Abū Ḥanīfa. The third: she has neither lodging nor maintenance. Mālik's proof is the hadith of Fāṭima bint Qays, that her husband divorced her irrevocably, and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to her: "You have no maintenance from him." From this it is derived that she has lodging but not maintenance. The proof of those who make lodging obligatory for her is the statement of ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb: "We will not abandon a verse of the Book of our Lord for the word of a woman. I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: 'She has lodging and maintenance.'" The proof of those who give her neither lodging nor maintenance is that in some narrations from her she said: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) did not give me maintenance or lodging."

His words ﴿where you dwell﴾ mean: lodge them in a place from among your dwellings; min is partitive. Qatāda's statement supports this: "If he has only one room, let her lodge in one of its corners." ﴿According to your means﴾: al-wujd is capacity and wealth; the meaning is: lodge them in accommodation within what you are able to afford. Grammatically, it is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to his words "where you dwell." In wujd it is permissible to vowel the wāw with a ḍamma, a fatḥa, or a kasra, and they have the same meaning, though the ḍamma is more common and more well known.

﴿And if they are pregnant, then spend upon them until they give birth.﴾ The scholars agreed on the obligation of maintenance during the waiting period for a pregnant divorced woman, in accordance with this verse, whether the divorce was revocable or irrevocable. They agreed that a non-pregnant divorced woman is entitled to maintenance during the waiting period if the divorce was revocable; if it was irrevocable, they differed concerning her maintenance, as we have mentioned. As for a woman whose husband has died while she is pregnant, there is no maintenance for her according to Mālik and the majority, because they held that this verse refers only to divorced women. Others said: she is entitled to maintenance from the estate.

﴿Then if they nurse for you, give them their wages.﴾ The meaning: if these divorced wives nurse your children, then give them the wage of nursing, which is maintenance and the other expenses, as mentioned in the books of jurisprudence.

﴿And confer among yourselves in kindness.﴾ This is addressed to men and women alike. The meaning is that each one should enjoin upon the other what is good: leniency, gentleness, and kindness. It was also said: the meaning of ā'tamirū is "consult one another," as in His words: ﴿Indeed, the eminent ones are conferring about you﴾ [al-Qaṣaṣ: 20].

﴿And if you disagree, then another woman will nurse for him.﴾ The meaning: if the mother is excessive toward the father regarding the wage of nursing and asks him for much, then the father may hire another woman to nurse his child at a rate that is easier for him, unless the infant will accept no breast other than his mother's; in that case she is compelled to nurse him for a wage equivalent to her customary rate and that of a wife (mithl) .

Let the wealthy man spend from his wealth (﴿Let the one of abundance spend from his abundance﴾). He commands that each person spend according to his circumstances; the husband should not be burdened with what he cannot bear, and the wife should not be left neglected, but the situation should be balanced. In the verse is evidence that maintenance (nafaqah) varies according to people's conditions, and this is the position of Malik (Malik ibn Anas), in contrast to Abu Hanifa, who considered it to be sufficiency (al-kifayah). As for one who is unable to maintain his wife, the position of Malik and al-Shafi'i is that she may be granted a divorce against him (yuṭallaqu ʿalayhi), in contrast to Abu Hanifa. If he is unable to provide clothing but not maintenance, then there are two opinions within the school (al-madhhab) regarding granting her divorce against him.

**[Ibn Juzayy, al-Tashil, on 65:8]**

﴿So We reckoned with her, a severe reckoning﴾. That is, We reckoned with its people. It has been said: this refers to the reckoning in the Hereafter, and likewise the punishment mentioned after it. And it has been said: it refers to this world, and this is the more preferred view, because He mentioned the punishment of the Hereafter afterwards in His words: ﴿Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment﴾ [al-Talaq: 10]; or because His words ﴿so We reckoned with her﴾ and ﴿and We punished her﴾ are in the past tense, so it is literally about what has occurred, and metaphorical about what has not occurred. So the meaning of "We reckoned with her" is: We seized them for their sins, and not one of their minor sins was overlooked for them. The "punishment" is their chastisement in this world, and "nukr" is the severe kind that its like has not been known.

﴿Indeed, Allah has sent down to you a reminder, a messenger﴾. The reminder here is the Qur'an, and the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ). The i'rab (grammatical analysis) of رسولاً (*rasulan*, "a messenger") is that it is the object of a suppressed verb, whose estimated meaning is: "He sent a messenger." This is the view chosen by Ibn 'Atiyya, and it is the most apparent of the opinions. It was said that the reminder and the messenger together are both intended to mean the Qur'an, and that "the messenger" on this view means "the message" (al-risalah). It was said that both are intended to mean the Qur'an, with an elided noun, its estimated meaning being ذكراً ذا رسول (*dhikran dha rasul*, "a reminder possessing a messenger"). It was said that رسولاً (*rasulan*) is the object of the verbal noun which is الذكر (*al-dhikr*, "the reminder"). Al-Zamakhshari said: "The messenger is Jibril, a substitute (badal) for the reminder, because he descended with it, or it was named a reminder because of his frequent remembrance of Allah." All of this is far-fetched.

Commentary of Ibn Juzayy (al-Tashil) on surah 65, verse 12:

﴿And of the earth, their like﴾ There is no disagreement that the heavens are seven. As for the earth, scholars differ concerning it. It is said that they are seven earths, based on the apparent meaning of this verse, and on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever usurps a span of land, it will be hung around his neck from the seven earths on the Day of Resurrection." And it is said that there is only one earth. So His saying ﹙their like﹚ according to the first view means similarity in number, and according to the second view means similarity in the greatness of the body, the abundance of inhabitation, and other things. The first view is more preponderant. ﴿The command descends among them﴾ It may be that by "the command" is meant the revelation, or the rulings of God and His decree for His creation.
